Unlike spoken languages, where prosody and tone convey emotion, sign languages rely on a complex interplay of facial expressions, hand movements, and body language, all of which can serve both linguistic and affective purposes. The EmoSign dataset comprises 200 ASL video clips, each annotated with sentiment ratings, the presence and intensity of ten distinct emotion categories, and open-ended descriptions of specific emotion cues. These annotations were provided by three Deaf ASL signers with professional interpretation experience, ensuring cultural relevance and accuracy. The paper emphasizes the need for new architectures that can disentangle the grammatical and affective functions of visual cues in sign languages, ultimately aiming to inspire the development of more nuanced and accurate emotion-aware models for sign language communication. The authors acknowledge the limitations of the dataset size and discuss future directions for expanding the dataset and improving model performance. The work is significant in that it provides a much-needed resource for the field of sign language emotion recognition, a domain that has been relatively under-explored compared to spoken language emotion recognition.
